By Alex Lennane
25 November 2026
Some airlines are agreeing alternative liability terms with larger freight forwarders under IATA’s revised direct air waybill (DAWB) framework, but smaller firms have little leverage to secure similar arrangements, the Airforwarders Association (AfA) has warned.
“If an airline says no, the forwarder either accepts the default terms or moves the cargo to another carrier,” AfA chief executive Steve Smith told The Loadstar .
“A global standard shouldn’t only work for companies big enough to negotiate their way out of it.”
Under the framework, effective since 1 July, a forwarder tendering cargo as agent for a shipper named on the airline’s air waybill assumes the shipper obligations that would apply if it were shipping in its own name, unless it agrees alternative bilateral terms with the carrier.
Mr Smith said some airlines were agreeing terms with larger forwarding customers. But negotiating separately with a dozen carriers, often through general sales agents, was not a realistic solution for a small or midsized forwarder with limited bargaining power.
“Since July, members have told us they can’t be sure which terms apply from one airline to the next,” he said. “Some have been asked to accept the new default without a separate agreement in place.”
He added: “Airlines don’t benefit from a patchwork either, because it adds paperwork on their side too.”
IATA declined to answer The Loadstar’s questions about the associations’ legal objections, whether it would consider revising the framework, or the status of the review requested by FIATA. It also declined to say whether it knew of claims under the revised provisions or alternative bilateral agreements.
Its refusal leaves those questions unanswered as forwarder associations seek changes to rules already in force across its member airlines.
In September, however, IATA told The Loadstar the provisions applied across member airlines and that carriers and forwarders could agree different terms.
It said the changes addressed a safety-related liability gap that left airlines exposed to improperly prepared cargo where they had little or no relationship with the underlying shipper.
Mr Smith said there was no reliable industry figure for DAWB usage. They accounted for a minority of volume for most forwarders, but were used where the underlying shipper needed to appear on the airline’s own document.
Examples included letters of credit and other trade-finance paperwork, certain export-control and customs requirements, and shipments booked through a forwarder using the shipper’s own airline rates.
“Even a small share matters, because the exposure applies to every shipment, and smaller forwarders are least able to absorb a single large claim,” he said.
AfA was unaware of any claims, insurance exclusions or premium increases linked to the revised provisions. But Mr Smith said the association wanted to address the exposure before a serious incident.
“We would rather fix the framework now than wait for a serious incident, such as a concealed dangerous goods case, to test it in court. By then a forwarder could be facing a claim its insurance doesn’t cover.”
In September, World Insurance told The Loadstar most forwarder liability policies already covered companies acting as both agents and principals, although forwarders should check that their cover adequately addressed the expanded liability.
AfA and the National Customs Brokers & Forwarders Association of America have published a joint white paper opposing the framework, with contributions from their Australian counterpart and support from the Canadian association. FIATA reiterated its call for a comprehensive industry review on Monday.
Mr Smith said the amendments should have awaited the review requested through FIATA.
“We expect to be part of these discussions before changes are made,” he said.
“We gave IATA notice before we published, and we’ve shared the paper with the International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations (FIATA) and with airlines directly. We’d welcome a seat at the review FIATA has asked IATA to convene.”
AfA wants the named shipper’s obligations to remain with that shipper by default, with forwarders responsible for their screening and security duties, the information they enter, their handling and customer checks.
“Airlines should keep full recourse against a forwarder that falls short on any of those. And it should be one default across carriers, not different terms on every airline,” Mr Smith said.
The white paper argues that the revised framework conflicts with the Montreal Convention. In September, HFW partner Matthew Gore told The Loadstar the provisions did not directly contradict the convention, although they could significantly expand a forwarder’s contractual exposure to the airline.
More recently, he said a UK industry association he had spoken to saw little change for most UK cargo, which generally moves under house air waybills, with forwarders already contracting directly with airlines under master air waybills.
Mr Gore had personally seen neither a claim tested under the revised provisions nor bilateral alternatives suggesting a settled market practice had emerged.
Mr Smith said AfA was not planning a legal challenge.
“Whatever the interpretation, we believe it is poor policy to put the risk on the party with the least control over the cargo, and we urge IATA to take that practical reality into account.”
AfA would continue pursuing changes with IATA and individual airlines, he added.
“If the framework doesn’t change, we’ll keep working with airlines one by one and keep our members informed on contracts and insurance.”
